newsitem.title: USA: Leaders decry racism in Chicago attacks.
newsitem.headline: Leaders decry racism in Chicago attacks.

text.p: Chicago's mayor, the leader of the Catholic Church and community activists raised their voices against racism on Tuesday after two incidents including the near-fatal beating of a black youth allegedly by whites.

"Three thugs. That's all they are," Mayor Richard Daley said of the three white teenagers accused of slamming 13-year-old Lenard Clark's head into a wall and administering a beating on Friday that left the black youth unconscious four days later.
"They're three thugs that beat up an innocent 13-year-old boy riding a bike," Daley said on a visit to Clark's bedside.
Police said the three alleged attackers -- two students at De La Salle Catholic high school and a recent graduate -- later bragged that they had taken "care of the niggers in the neighbourhood."

Several witnesses including other whites pointed out the three -- two high school juniors, Victor Jasas, 17, and Frank Caruso, 18, and 1996 graduate Michael Kwidzinski, 19 -- supposedly made a habit of harassing passers-by, especially blacks.

They were charged with attempted murder, aggravated battery and committing a hate crime and were released on Monday after posting 10 percent of their bonds set at $100,000 for Jasas and Caruso and $150,000 for Kwidzinski. Their lawyers denied they were involved in the attack, but said they may have witnessed it.

"Learning that these suspects ... were released from police custody on such low bonds cheapens the price of hate crime," the Rev. Jesse Jackson said. "I am deeply disturbed by these patterns of racism and hatred in our city."
The leader of Chicago's Catholic Archdiocese, Bishop Raymond Goedert, also announced he would form a task force to address racism in the church's schools.

Jackson and Goedert referred to a recent incident that roiled the city where students at another Brother Rice Catholic school on the South Side chanted "Buckwheat" and possibly other racist epithets during a basketball game against a rival school with black players. A few black students at Brother Rice later said some staff members and students mistreated them because of their race.

Friday's attack occurred near Daley's boyhood neighbourhood of Bridgeport on the city's South Side, a largely white enclave with an increasing number of Hispanic and Asian residents but few blacks. Daley also attended De La Salle.
"Don't make me the issue. I'm outraged by this," Daley said, when asked about any connection with the defendants.
